description: We’re building A.R.E.S., a Mars survival map that combines terrain, hazards, resources, and crew conditions to help astronauts plan safer routes and return options.
summary:
This project is a proposed crewed Mars exploration mission focused on the scientific investigation of Acidalia Planitia. Its accompanying web-based platform serves as a centralised digital mission-support system, integrating geographical exploration, crew monitoring, environmental awareness and mission coordination.

Mission Objectives: Investigate Martian geology, identify potential water-ice resources, study environmental conditions for extraterrestrial lifeform, assess region's suitability for future human exploration and habitation.

Key Features:

- Interactive Mars Mapping: Visualises Acidalia Planitia, supporting geographical awareness, exploration-site identification and route planning.
- Crew Vital Monitoring: Provides a unified dashboard for monitoring the health parameters of all four astronauts.
- Environmental Monitoring: Integrates surface temperature, atmospheric conditions and other environmental information relevant to astronaut safety.
- Mission Coordination: Consolidates scientific, geographical and crew-related information into one accessible interface.
The platform aims to address critical challenges of Martian exploration, including unfamiliar terrain, extreme temperatures, environmental hazards, astronaut health risks, limited resources and communication delays with Earth. By centralising mission information, A.R.E.S. supports informed decision-making, improves operational awareness, facilitates safer exploration and reduces information fragmentation.
details:
A.R.E.S. – Walk on Mars. Come home safe.

What it does

A.R.E.S. is a field map and EVA planner for a crew exploring a real Martian site: a crater in Chryse Planitia (28.43° N, 319.77° E). We built a 3D model of the ground from NASA orbital data. A planner uses it to lay out a 7-sol mission: where the pressurised rover drives, where the crew stops, who does what, and when they must turn back.

How it works

The 3D terrain comes from MOLA elevation data (200 m). CTX imagery (about 20 m) sits on top, with THEMIS day and night infrared (100 m) filling the gaps and HiRISE strips (0.5 m) adding detail. The Mars colour is measured from the Viking colour mosaic, not painted on. Every layer names its source and resolution.

The route planner picks the stops and checks each leg against slope limits, rover energy and time windows. Every number is stored with its source, and values we could not measure are marked as placeholders.

For each of Sols 1 to 7 there is a running Mars-time clock (LMST) with rover telemetry, battery level, crew timelines, experiment checklists and field data forms.

In the Mission view the rover drives the planned route, seen from a chase camera, the driver's eye or the whole route. A crew view shows the real horizon at standing height.

The Rover view shows the team's CAD model of the MARS-X HORIZON rover in each mode: driving, drilling, rock crawling, storm stand and the cabin. The habitat appears on the map at true scale.

Vitals gives full-screen monitoring of crew, habitat, rover and supplies. A dust storm test cuts solar power by 30%.

The Log records every decision and needs role-based approval. Paper sheets print out for when the screens go dark.

At sign-in the user picks a role: Commander, EVA lead, science, medic, Mission Control or the A.R.E.S. agent. Each role sees its own tasks.

Benefits and impact

The most important question on any EVA is "can we get back?". A.R.E.S. answers it before the crew leaves the airlock, and keeps answering it minute by minute. It turns raw orbital data into go, slow down or turn-back decisions a tired crew can act on. Being honest about data is part of the safety: the map shows how sharp each dataset is and marks the ground no orbiter has imaged well. The same workflow fits Moon and Mars analog missions, astronaut training and teaching planetary science.

Tools and technologies

We wrote the app in JavaScript with React 19, three.js, React Three Fiber and drei, and built it with Vite. Vitest runs the automated tests and oxlint checks the code. Node.js scripts processed the data, and the rover and habitat models were made in Blender and exported as glTF. The data comes from MRO CTX and HiRISE, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA and the Viking colour mosaic. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages and runs in any browser with no install and no server.

Creativity

A.R.E.S. is more than a map viewer. It joins real terrain, a mission planner, a running Mars clock, crew roles and the rover's CAD model in one tool. You can stand on the real crater and see its true horizon. Paper sheets are a deliberate fallback for emergencies. Being open about data limits is built into the design, not hidden.

What we considered

We weighed safety first: slope, energy and turn-back margins. We kept the data honest, with no invented numbers. For clarity under pressure, each screen has one main focus. Each crew member sees and approves only what their role allows. If the systems fail, there are printed sheets and an audit trail. And the app is open to everyone: https://02mandavi.github.io/ares-map/
